_: The feature cards: one entry per feature, and one per part of a feature. main.js shows an entry in the object card when its object is clicked or it's chosen from the panel's Features list; Explore features marks the objects; scripts/14_check_features.mjs checks every entry has its fields, links to an object and names a demo or action that exists. Objects: addon:<id> (an add-on built in addons.js), part:<name> (a part of the room models), placed:<type> (an item from Place items), node:<name> (a named object, such as a wardrobe compartment, which counts only while its door is open), lights (the ceiling lights of the scheme in use), switch (the smart-glass wall switch). After a |, a condition on the room's choices: the object counts for this entry only then. The first object is where Explore's marker goes. A feature worked from a control above the room, with no object of its own, names that control's id in `control` instead. Evidence is either 'Expected, not shown.' or a line with its strength and sources from options.json (sourcesFrom: a group, or group:option). Nothing here is measured: every reading and status on a card is simulated.

features.name: Adaptive circadian lighting
features.purpose: Room light that follows the day: cool and bright by day, warm and dim in the evening.
features.how: Choose Circadian under Lighting. Its white light is tunable. The colour follows the room's solar time: warm at dawn, coolest from 10 am to 3 pm, warm again by 7 pm. From 6:30 pm to 9:30 pm it dims to well under half. The reading light and the examination task light keep their own switches.
features.benefit: A clearer day and night, and less bright light when the patient should be asleep.
features.awake: It follows the day, and the reading light is still there for a book.
features.sedated: It follows the day all the same. Staff set the light for care.
features.limits: Light alone isn't shown to prevent delirium. Care comes first: Clinical and Emergency-ready modes switch to full, neutral light.

evidence.text: Mixed. A pilot in redesigned rooms with dynamic light saw less delirium, but the rooms changed in other ways too. A randomised trial of bright dynamic light alone found no effect.
evidence.strength: Observational pilot; randomised trial, stopped early for futility

features.name: Light across 24 hours
features.purpose: A plan for the room's light and blinds over a whole day, in four phases: morning daylight, afternoon comfort, evening wind-down and night sleep.
features.how: Open it from Time of day, then drag the hour along a 24-hour timeline, or step it with the arrow keys. The room shows the circadian light and the blinds at that hour, and every change takes an hour or more. Quiet hours, 10 pm to 6 am, are marked. Play the day runs through the 24 hours once, in 24 seconds, and stops.
features.benefit: A clear day and night, with gradual changes and a dark, quiet night.
features.awake: The reading light and the blinds are still there when the patient asks.
features.sedated: The plan runs all the same, and staff set the light for care.
features.limits: A plan, not a measurement, and light alone isn't shown to prevent delirium. Clinical and Emergency-ready are the staff override and always win. It changes no choice or link, and closing it puts the time back.

evidence.text: Mixed. A pilot in redesigned rooms with dynamic light saw less delirium, but the rooms changed in other ways too. A randomised trial of bright dynamic light alone found no effect.
evidence.strength: Observational pilot; randomised trial, stopped early for futility

features.name: Privacy system
features.purpose: Privacy at the glazed front and the window when the patient needs it. Staff can end it at once.
features.how: With smart glass on the glazed front, the wall switch or Privacy mode turns the glass opaque, so no fabric curtain is needed. Privacy mode also lowers the window blinds halfway. A curtain or blinds front is closed by hand. Emergency-ready clears the glass.
features.benefit: Dignity during care, washing and rest, without a curtain to launder.
features.awake: The patient can ask for privacy, and for it to end.
features.sedated: Staff use it during care, and clear the glass to look in.
features.limits: Opaque glass hides the patient from the corridor, so staff decide when it's used. In an isolation room the door still needs its seal and pressure tests.

evidence.text: Memorial Sloan Kettering's ICU replaced curtains with switchable glass and reported easier cleaning and better infection control.

features.name: Patient orientation display
features.purpose: The TV can show the weekday, the date, the time of day and whether it's day or night, with a few calm lines beside them: where the patient is, visiting confirmed by staff, and what's planned. Large enough to read from the bed.
features.how: Choose Orientation under Entertainment. The time comes from the room's own sun, and the screen is darker at night. Beside it: a line about where the patient is, visiting information marked as confirmed by staff, a non-urgent plan, and a recovery note when the patient is recovering. Family can add a line, if staff confirm it. It never shows a name, a diagnosis or care information.
features.benefit: Knowing the day and the time without having to ask.
features.awake: Readable from the pillow. Patient view shows what the patient sees.
features.sedated: It stays calm, and darker at night, with nothing that asks for attention.
features.limits: It makes no claim about delirium or sleep. The lines are samples: a real screen would show only what staff have confirmed, and never patient details.

features.name: Nature and environmental display
features.purpose: Calm, natural things to look at from the bed: a scene on the TV, a sky on the ceiling, a digital aquarium and a printed leaf panel.
features.how: Each is its own choice. The TV's scene and the aquarium are original animations drawn in the page. The sky is a lit panel above the bed. The leaf panel is placed from Place items. None brings soil, water or animals into the room.
features.benefit: Something restful to look at, instead of equipment and a blank ceiling.
features.awake: The patient can choose what's on, or turn it off.
features.sedated: Staff choose, and keep it still and quiet.
features.limits: Emergency-ready turns the screens off. Living plants and fish tanks stay out of patient-care areas, as CDC guidance advises.

features.name: TV nature scene
features.purpose: An original animation on the TV: desert dunes under a slowly moving sun.
features.how: Choose On under Entertainment, TV. It's drawn in the page at a slow frame rate, and only while the TV is in view.
features.benefit: A slow, natural scene to rest the eyes on.
features.limits: Placeholder content, not real footage. Emergency-ready turns it off.

features.name: Sky ceiling
features.purpose: A printed sky on the ceiling above the bed, lit from behind.
features.how: Choose Printed sky under Ceiling above the bed. The panel is 3 by 2.2 m, centred over the bed, and it glows without the room lights.
features.benefit: Something to look up at that isn't a light fitting or a ceiling grid.
features.limits: A real panel needs a wipe-clean face and a fixing the ceiling can take.

features.name: Digital aquarium
features.purpose: Animated fish on a wall screen, with no water, fish or servicing in the room.
features.how: Choose Digital screen under Aquarium. The fish are drawn in the page, and move only while the screen is in view.
features.benefit: The calm of watching fish, with nothing to clean or keep alive.
features.limits: CDC guidance says to avoid fish tanks in patient-care areas, which is why it's a screen. Emergency-ready turns it off.

features.name: Biophilic wall panel
features.purpose: Greenery without soil or water: a printed leaf scene behind a sealed, wipe-clean acrylic face. Living plants stay outside the glass.
features.how: Place it from Place items, on any clear stretch of wall. It's about 0.9 by 1.2 m, centred 1.7 m up, clear of wall ledges.
features.benefit: Green to look at, from something that's cleaned like any other surface.
features.limits: CDC guidance says not to allow fresh flowers or potted plants in patient-care areas for immunosuppressed patients, so real plants stay outside.

features.name: Built-in sliding wardrobe
features.purpose: Compact, organised storage for the patient's clothing, belongings and daily necessities, built in floor to ceiling against the back wall, clear of the entry route.
features.how: Two flush sliding doors on two tracks, so one side opens at a time: the left door runs behind the right. Behind them, a compartment for each use: daily essentials on a shelf at eye level, a lockable box for valuables, room for a bag, and a rail for clothes. A low-glare light comes on inside when a door opens. Flush end and filler panels make it read as joinery, and a fixed panel over the doors hides the track and leaves no top for dust. A real one would need the wall, services, infection-control requirements and emergency clearances checked.
features.benefit: Belongings kept organised, private and easy to find, and out of sight, so the room looks less cluttered.
features.awake: The patient knows where their things are, and can ask for them.
features.sedated: Nurses or authorised caregivers reach belongings for the patient.
features.limits: It takes about the same floor area as the freestanding wardrobe it replaced: what it adds is height, easier cleaning and a tidier look. A design concept: no inventory display or electronic lock is modelled.

features.name: Clothing
features.purpose: A dedicated area for clean patient clothing and personal garments, keeping belongings organised and separate from clinical supplies.
features.how: A hanging rail behind the right-hand door, with room for shoes below it.
features.benefit: Clothes kept clean, together and ready to wear.
features.limits: Patient clothing only: clinical supplies are kept elsewhere.

features.name: Daily essentials
features.purpose: An accessible shelf for items such as glasses, books and approved everyday necessities.
features.how: A shelf at eye level behind the left-hand door, about 1.5 m up, within reach of someone standing.
features.benefit: Less searching for the things used every day.
features.limits: What may be kept at the bedside is the ward's decision.

features.name: Personal belongings
features.purpose: A section for bags and other permitted belongings, keeping the room organised.
features.how: Space on the cabinet floor behind the left-hand door, for a bag or a small case.
features.benefit: A bag has its own place, instead of standing on the floor.
features.limits: Only permitted belongings: the ward decides what can stay.

features.name: Secure valuables
features.purpose: A separately controlled box for permitted valuables.
features.how: A lockable box on a low shelf behind the left-hand door. In this model the keypad is drawn on, and nothing locks.
features.benefit: Valuables kept apart from everyday things, out of sight.
features.limits: In real hospital use, storage and access must follow institutional security policies.

features.name: Cabinet lighting
features.purpose: Low-glare light inside the cabinet, for finding belongings in dim conditions.
features.how: A warm strip under the inside top. In this model it comes on while a door is open.
features.benefit: Staff can find things without turning on the room lights.
features.limits: It can be turned off, so it doesn't disturb the patient's rest. No switch or sensor is modelled.

features.name: Sliding doors
features.purpose: Flush sliding doors, which open without swinging out into the room.
features.how: Two doors on two tracks, hung from above behind the fixed panel, with a guide at the foot. One side opens at a time.
features.benefit: Nothing swings into the space where staff work.
features.limits: The freestanding wardrobe it replaced had sliding doors too, so the mechanism isn't new.

features.name: Patient states
features.purpose: The room follows the patient: sedated or unresponsive, awake, or recovering. A control above the room, beside the room modes.
features.how: Sedated: steady light by the time of day, a little lower, and nothing on the patient's screen; staff set comfort and see the positioning reminder, line status and noise. Awake: the room as configured, with the patient's own controls, communication, privacy and family. Recovering: the orientation screen first, light by the time of day, simple choices. Changes ease over a few seconds. The room modes stay as they are: Clinical and Emergency-ready are the staff override and always win.
features.benefit: What the patient sees and hears suits what they can take in.
features.awake: The patient's own controls and choices.
features.sedated: Steady light and no entertainment. Comfort is set by staff.
features.limits: Staff decide the state: the room never works it out from the patient. It changes no alarm, device or clinical setting, and it changes no choice or link.

features.name: Communication board
features.purpose: Large buttons for a patient who can't speak: I need help, I am in pain, I feel cold, I feel hot, I need repositioning, I want to contact my family, I need a nurse.
features.how: On the bedside tablet, or on any bedside screen. Eleven requests, each in English and Arabic: the first seven, then I need water, I can't sleep, I need help communicating, and a request for privacy. Three ways to choose: touch; a single switch, while a highlight steps through the buttons; or gaze, where a look held on a button chooses it. Here the switch and gaze are simulated. Each request goes to a nurse-side list with the time, in both languages, with a line that a nurse confirms anything clinical in person, and stays there until a nurse acknowledges it. From a privacy request, the nurse can turn on Privacy.
features.benefit: A patient who can't speak can still ask for what they need.
features.awake: The patient chooses by touch, a switch or gaze.
features.sedated: Not offered: staff watch for signs instead.
features.limits: Simulated. It does not replace a certified nurse-call system: a real one is wired, tested and maintained to its own standard. No request leaves this page. The Arabic was written for this demo: a native reader must check it.

features.name: Personal comfort passport
features.purpose: A sample record of what a patient would like: light, temperature, music or quiet, a nature scene, family photographs, privacy, how they communicate, and entertainment.
features.how: Recorded with the patient or their family. It keeps the patient's preferences apart from the settings the care team controls, and shows how each preference is used or held back in each patient state. Save it in this browser, or restore the sample. It's its own record: Suggest a room and PACS keep theirs.
features.benefit: Staff can see at a glance what the patient likes, even when the patient can't say.
features.awake: The patient's preferences are used.
features.sedated: Most are held back; staff use some, if they judge them right.
features.limits: A sample for a made-up patient, with no name. Temperature is shown, not applied: no approved limits were supplied. Saved only in this browser, never sent.

features.name: Family connection
features.purpose: Family close by on the bedside screens: photographs, a video call, a voice message, a personal scene, familiar music and a line on the orientation screen.
features.how: Drawn photographs stand in for real ones. The video call and voice message are simulated: shown, not played, because there's no real voice to use. The personal scene goes on the TV, and familiar music plays as demo sound, only when pressed. Staff have Quiet now, which turns all stimulation off, sound included. For an unresponsive patient it offers only what staff allow.
features.benefit: Familiar faces, voices and music, when the patient can take them in.
features.awake: The patient and family choose.
features.sedated: Only what staff allow.
features.limits: No photograph is uploaded, no camera or microphone is used, and nothing is sent. A real call would need the hospital's approved system.

features.name: Sound-level sensor
features.purpose: A closed door keeps a patient's voice in. This sensor concept gives that hearing back: it would recognise a groan or a call for help and put a notice in front of the nurse outside, who looks in through the glass before deciding to enter. Simulated here by the two buttons.

W1.purpose: A closed isolation door keeps the air in, and the patient's voice with it. This sensor concept gives that hearing back: it would recognise a groan or a call for help and put a notice in front of the nurse outside, who looks in through the glass before deciding to enter. Simulated here by the two buttons.

features.how: The sensor would classify sounds on the device. A call for help asks for a look now. One groan asks for a look when the nurse can, and a third within a minute for a look now. Its light changes colour, and the notice says what was heard. The nurse decides whether to go in.
features.benefit: A patient behind a closed door can still be heard.
features.awake: A call for help reaches the nurse without a button.
features.sedated: Ventilated or sedated patients may make no sound. Quiet is never a sign that all is well.

features.name: Room comfort control
features.purpose: A wall-mounted temperature and humidity control concept. It is not connected to room equipment or patient measurements. The air behind it is cleaned in the plant room, out of sight:
features.how: The Comfort systems section has two SIMULATED sliders, for temperature and humidity. They change this control's status light: blue when cool, amber when warm. Nothing is heated, cooled or measured.
features.benefit: One place by the door where staff can see the room's comfort settings.
features.limits: No hospital-approved temperature limits were supplied, so nothing is set from here. Cleaning the air is the plant room's job.

features.name: Daylight sensor
features.purpose: A small light sensor on the window sill. It tells Comfort mode and PACS whether daylight is coming in.
features.how: By day, Comfort mode lowers the blinds against glare. After sunset there's no glare to block, so Comfort mode and PACS leave the blinds alone and change only the lighting. In this model the sun's height at the room's solar hour stands in for its reading.
features.benefit: The blinds don't close on an evening view for no reason.
features.limits: A concept: it isn't connected to anything, and it reads nothing here.

features.name: Acoustic comfort mode
features.purpose: A picture of the room's sound: where it comes from, where it's loudest, and what acoustic fittings would change. Simulated.
features.how: Press Acoustic comfort mode above the room. Labels mark six simulated sources: monitor tones, infusion pumps, the ventilator, equipment fans, the door and talk in the corridor, and the two loudest at the pillow are marked. A sound map colours the floor, a ring marks a quiet zone round the bed, and the sound sensor shows a level. Without fittings and With fittings compare the room. The map uses the simplest distance rule: 6 dB quieter each time the distance from a source doubles. Demo sound plays only when asked.
features.benefit: Shows where the room's noise comes from, so a team can see what to change first.
features.awake: A restful sound can play, if staff decide it suits the patient. It never plays over a notice or an alarm.
features.sedated: Nothing here touches the patient's equipment: its alarms and settings stay as they are.
features.limits: Not a measurement: no microphone is used, and nothing listens. Every level is illustrative, and the fittings' effect is made up. Critical alarms are always sounding and visible, and the comfort system has no control over them.

evidence.text: Every ICU in a five-unit study was louder than WHO's hospital guideline, which its authors judged out of reach in an ICU. The fittings' effect is expected, not shown.
evidence.strength: Observational study of five UK ICUs

features.name: Acoustic panels
features.purpose: Wipe-clean panels on the wall and ceiling that absorb some of the sound bouncing round the room.
features.how: Two panels on the family zone's back wall and three ceiling tiles over it, clear of the vents, the lights and the bed. A sealed face over the absorber, wiped like any other surface. Choose them under Acoustic fittings.
features.benefit: Less of every sound bounces back into the room.
features.limits: Their effect in Acoustic comfort mode is made up. A real one needs infection-control and manufacturer sign-off.

features.name: Acoustic partition
features.purpose: The glazed front in laminated acoustic glass, sealed all round: staff still see in, and less corridor talk comes through.
features.how: Laminated glass with a sound-damping layer, and seals round the opening. It stays clear glass, so the smart glass and the curtain still work. Choose it under Acoustic fittings.
features.benefit: Corridor talk stays outside, and the view in stays open.
features.limits: Its effect in Acoustic comfort mode is made up. A real one needs infection-control and manufacturer sign-off. An isolation room's door still needs its own seal and pressure tests.

features.name: Soft-close door and cabinets
features.purpose: Dampers that slow the door and cabinet doors over their last few centimetres, so they don't bang.
features.how: A damper at the head of the room's door, and in the wardrobe's track. The door still closes and seals by itself. Choose it under Acoustic fittings.
features.benefit: No bang when a door shuts at night.
features.limits: Its effect in Acoustic comfort mode is made up. A real one needs infection-control and manufacturer sign-off. It must never stop a door closing fully.

features.name: Vibration-damping mounts
features.purpose: Rubber isolators behind non-critical kit, here the TV, so a hum doesn't carry into the wall.
features.how: Isolators between the TV's bracket and the wall. Never on the monitor, the pumps, the ventilator or any medical device. Choose them under Acoustic fittings.
features.benefit: Less hum carried through the wall.
features.limits: Non-critical kit only. Their effect in Acoustic comfort mode is made up. A real one needs infection-control and manufacturer sign-off.

features.name: Pressure-awareness bed
features.purpose: A sensor grid in the mattress shows where the patient's weight bears, so staff can see when a position has been held too long. Simulated.
features.how: A grid of pressure cells under the sheet. Here the map is made up, from the usual teaching pictures of pressure points: it colours the mattress light, moderate or higher by relative load. A place under a higher load, held past the positioning plan's interval, is marked, and staff see Positioning assessment due until they dismiss it. Choose a position (on the back, turned left or right, or sitting up) and the map shifts. Staff check the lines before any move.
features.benefit: Staff can see where the weight bears, even under the bedding, and when a position has been held a long time.
features.awake: The patient moves by themselves, and the map follows.
features.sedated: Staff see the reminder, assess the skin and reposition by the plan.
features.limits: Simulated: not a measurement. It predicts no injury, and it never moves a patient: staff assess and reposition by the patient's own positioning plan. The bed and the figure in this model don't move, so the positions are shown on the map only.

features.name: Line clips and tags
features.purpose: A clip on each line's route round the patient, with a tag in its colour, and each line's slack shown before a move. Simulated.
features.how: Clips on the side rails' tops hold the IV line, the feeding tube and the ECG leads. A holder at the head end takes the respiratory circuit, and a guide on the bed frame takes the urinary drainage, never on a moving rail. In the bed panel's Lines, each line shows its slack in the position chosen: slack enough, less slack, or check this line. Before any move, staff check every line. Choose the clips under Bed in the options.
features.benefit: Each route stays where staff expect it, so a line is quicker to trace before a move.
features.awake: The lines stay clear of the patient's hands and the rails.
features.sedated: Staff check every line before turning the patient or moving the bed.
features.limits: Simulated: no tension, force or flow is worked out, and no line or device is monitored. The clips don't secure a line, and nothing here changes a real line, connector or device. APIS keeps its own tubing tab.

features.name: Ceiling tray
features.purpose: A calm ceiling over the bed: square tiles in a shallow tray, with a soft line of light round its edge.
features.how: The tray sits over the bed, clear of the ceiling lights, the pendant and the wardrobe. Its line of light takes the colour of the room's light, so with the circadian scheme it follows the day. A row of small downlights runs along the window side. With the printed sky on, the sky fits inside it. Choose it under Future ICU fittings.
features.benefit: The ceiling is what a patient lying in bed sees most. A tidy one, lit at its edges, is calmer to look at than bare fittings.
features.awake: The patient looks up at an even ceiling, with its line of light at the edges.
features.limits: A design concept. In this model its light adds no brightness: the room's own lights do that. A real one needs the ceiling's services, structure, access panels and infection-control requirements checked.

features.name: Staff panel
features.purpose: Information for the care team on the wall behind the bed head, where staff look and the patient can't.
features.how: One flush white panel with rounded corners, two wide screens and a thin line of light beneath. The pendant in front still carries the monitor, pumps and outlets. Its screens follow the smart clinical wall: in Clinical, made-up observations, care tasks and equipment, all marked simulated; otherwise a dark standby that shows nothing about the patient. Choose it under Future ICU fittings.
features.benefit: Tasks and equipment are at a glance at the bedside, so there's less walking to another screen.
features.awake: It's behind the patient's head, so it adds nothing to what they see.
features.limits: Simulated: its values are made up and fixed, not readings, and it never stands in for the patient monitor, which stays on the pendant, working, with its alarms unchanged. A real one needs integration, infection-control and regulatory review.

features.name: Patient wall
features.purpose: The wall the patient faces, made into one calm surface round the TV.
features.how: A flush white panel round the TV, with a strip of screen over it and a line of light beneath. The TV sits on its face, so the orientation screen, the nature scene and the damping mounts keep working. It follows the smart clinical wall: in Patient, the strip shows the care team by role and the day's plan, with two buttons that open the communication board and family connection; in Relaxation, a scene runs across the whole wall and the TV. Choose it under Future ICU fittings.
features.benefit: What a patient is meant to read is on the wall they face, not behind their head.
features.awake: The patient sees the TV and the strip over it from the pillow.
features.sedated: The strip stays still, with no buttons: nothing on it moves, flashes or asks for anything.
features.limits: Simulated: no real names, plans or times. Whether the strip can be read from the pillow depends on the patient's eyesight; Patient view shows the distance. A real one needs integration and infection-control review.

features.name: Clinician workstation
features.purpose: A desk for the care team in the room, by the window and out of the space round the bed.
features.how: A rounded white top on a timber-and-white cabinet, a screen and keyboard, a second screen on an arm, and a lit rail. It stands clear of the keep-clear areas, the door and the walking route to the bed. In W1 the visitor chair moves nearer the window to make room. Its screens show a made-up patient's dashboard, marked simulated, with no name or diagnosis. Open the workstation for its Nurse view and Doctor view, a task that lights where its things are, hands-free buttons, and in Emergency-ready the emergency equipment and the clear route to the bed. Choose it under Future ICU fittings.
features.benefit: Notes and tasks are at hand in the room, so there's less walking between workstations and less searching.
features.awake: Nothing about the patient is said aloud: the hands-free buttons answer on the screen only.
features.limits: Simulated: a made-up patient, made-up values and a scripted task list. Nothing listens: each hands-free button stands in for a spoken command. Its Emergency view is not a validated emergency protocol. It opens PACS, and doesn't copy or change it. A real one needs its place, power, data, infection-control and clinical review.

features.name: Bedside cabinet
features.purpose: A place near the bed for the patient's own small things: glasses, a phone, a book.
features.how: A cabinet with a rounded white top and a timber front, against the wall at the bed head on the window side: clear of the pendant, its outlets and the space round the bed. Choose it under Future ICU fittings.
features.benefit: Small belongings stay near the patient and off the overbed table.
features.awake: Family or staff hand the patient what's in it.
features.limits: A design concept. Clinical supplies are kept apart from it. A real one needs its finishes reviewed for infection control.

features.name: Smart clinical wall
features.purpose: One wall, more than one purpose: the staff panel and the patient wall show what each person needs now. Staff get observations, tasks and equipment; the patient gets the day, the time, the care team and the plan; at rest, a calm scene.
features.how: One switch, under Smart clinical wall: Clinical, Patient or Relaxation. Clinical fills the staff panel at the bed head with made-up heart rate, oxygen saturation, blood pressure, breathing rate and temperature, care tasks and equipment, and leaves the patient the day and the time. Patient shows the orientation screen on the TV, the care team by role and the day's plan over it, and two buttons that open the communication board and family connection. Relaxation puts a scene across the patient wall. The room's modes move it too: Clinical turns it to Clinical, Comfort to Relaxation, and Emergency-ready turns the patient wall off, and every scene with it. It needs the staff panel and the patient wall, under Future ICU fittings.
features.benefit: Information organised by who needs it and when, on screens built into the wall instead of more devices round the bed.
features.awake: From the pillow, in Patient view, the time, the care team and the plan are large enough to read, and the two buttons open the bedside screens.
features.sedated: No buttons and no prompts: the patient wall shows the time or a scene, and staff use the staff panel.
features.limits: Simulated: every value is made up and fixed, and the staff panel never stands in for the bedside monitor, which keeps running with its alarms unchanged. Observations show only in Clinical, so visitors don't see them. A real wall needs clinical integration, infection-control and regulatory review.

features.name: Transform my environment
features.purpose: Bringing the outside world into intensive care: the patient chooses a forest, the ocean, mountains, the desert, a garden, a clear sky or a night sky, and the room takes it on.
features.how: One choice, under Smart clinical wall, sets the patient wall, the ceiling above the bed and the room's light together, and changes slowly, over a few seconds. Off goes back to how the room was. Each scene is drawn in code, in the style of the TV's desert, the sky ceiling and the feature walls. Without the patient wall, the scene shows on the TV. The patient's state and a room mode come first, Quiet now takes the scene off the wall, and Emergency-ready turns every scene off.
features.benefit: A safe choice about their own surroundings, for a patient who has few.
features.awake: The patient chooses a scene, or asks for one on the communication board, and can always go back to how the room was.
features.sedated: Staff or family can choose a calm scene. Nothing in it asks for attention.
features.limits: Drawn scenes, not footage, and a concept: it makes no claim about sleep, delirium or recovery. Living plants stay outside the glass. A real system needs infection-control, electrical and clinical review.

features.name: Room modes
features.purpose: The room changes together: one choice of mode moves the light, the blinds, the glass, the wall screens, scenes, sound, the bedside screens, notices and overlays, in step.
features.how: Seven modes above the room: As set, Comfort, Privacy, Clinical, Family visit, Cleaning, and Emergency-ready on its own. One table says what each mode does in each system, and five levels of priority settle any clash, highest first: clinical safety and emergency access; what staff have switched on; patient communication; patient comfort preferences; decoration and presentation. A lower level never overrides a higher one, so a scene the patient chose gives way to Clinical, and everything gives way to Emergency-ready. Each mode's note says in one line what changed, and that medical alarms always stay on. No mode changes a choice: As set puts the room back.
features.benefit: Staff change the room for what's happening now with one press, and nothing has to be put back by hand.
features.awake: The patient's own choices, like a scene, come back when a mode ends.
features.sedated: The modes work the same. The patient's state sits under them: staff modes always win.
features.limits: A demonstration of the idea. No mode touches an alarm, a medical device or the bedside monitor. The table and its levels are this model's own, set as data; a real room's would be set by the hospital and tested.

features.name: Family visit
features.purpose: A mode for when family come: the room warms, privacy is as the patient asked, and family connection is on the wall they face.
features.how: Family visit, above the room. The light goes warm and ambient. Smart glass on the glazed front softens to a frost, unless the patient's passport says they'd rather see out, so staff can still see in. Family connection goes on the TV, with a scene round it on the patient wall if the patient chose one. Staff can end it at any moment, and Emergency-ready clears everything.
features.benefit: Time with family feels less like a ward, without hiding the patient from the care team.
features.awake: It follows the patient's own passport: how much privacy, and a scene if they chose one.
features.sedated: Family connection offers only what staff allow, as it always does for an unresponsive patient.
features.limits: Simulated: the photographs are drawn placeholders and the message is made up. Softened glass is a concept: a real front needs its privacy level and staff sight lines agreed with the care team.

features.name: Cleaning
features.purpose: A mode for the room between patients: bright light, the bed empty, and the surfaces that are touched most marked one after another.
features.how: Cleaning, above the room. The patient figure goes, and comes back when the mode ends. The light goes bright, the screens go off, and a checklist comes up: hands first, then the bed rails and controls, the overbed table, the monitor and pump screens, the ventilator, the pendant, the wall controls and handles, the chairs, and hands again. Each step lights what it covers in the room; tick it, and the next lights. The hand-hygiene point is the basin in the room. No airflow is drawn, because the grilles are hidden: the checklist links to the ventilation plan.
features.benefit: Cleaning in a set order, with nothing missed, and the equipment that needs it marked.
features.awake: Not for an occupied room: the bed is empty.
features.sedated: Not for an occupied room: the bed is empty.
features.limits: An order to show the idea, not a cleaning protocol: products, contact times and the order of work are the infection-control team's. Finishing the checklist says it's finished, and never that the room is clean or disinfected.

features.name: Transform the ICU
features.purpose: Today's room, then the room of the future arriving a piece at a time: the difference is how the room works, not only how it looks.
features.how: Under View, Transform the ICU plays Compare with today's room as a short story. It starts from today's room, every option at its default, then adds the Future ICU's pieces one after another: the floor and the light, the ceiling tray, the wall screens, the desk and the cabinet, a scene, and a room mode moving them together. When it ends, the visitor's own room comes back exactly.
features.benefit: Seeing what changes, one piece at a time, and why each piece is there.
features.awake: The patient's own choices, like a scene, are part of the story.
features.sedated: Nothing in it is for a patient: it's a presentation of the room.
features.limits: Today's room is a typical arrangement, not every ICU, and the equipment is a typical ICU kit, not SSMC's inventory. A demo: it changes no choice or link.

features.name: Digital twin
features.purpose: A digital reflection of the room: its hidden state made visible, so the space, equipment, environment and work can be seen together.
features.how: Open the digital twin. Seven systems, each read in words and lit in the room when chosen: the bed, the ceiling with its sensors and light, the walls with their screens, privacy and comfort control, storage, equipment, the floor and its clear areas, and the mode in force with its row of the mode table. Above them, room health in five separate parts: environmental comfort, equipment organisation, access clearance, communication readiness and the cleaning checklist. Each part says whether there's anything to look at. It reads the room as it is: change the mode, the patient's state or a choice, and it changes.
features.benefit: One place to see how the room is set up right now, without walking round it.
features.awake: It shows whether the board, the wall's buttons and family connection are offered to the patient.
features.sedated: It shows the bed's position, its reminder and the lines, which staff check most.
features.limits: A concept: it reads only this model, with its simulated and illustrative values, and monitors nothing. The five parts are never added into a score, and it shows no vital signs, which are PACS's. Its clear areas are this model's own, not hospital rules.

features.name: Room intelligence
features.purpose: A room that notices when help may be needed: it would help staff see a possible safety concern while keeping the room calm and uncluttered.
features.how: Three flush sensors on the ceiling: over the bed, inside the door and over the middle of the room. Open room intelligence and activate it to see the floor each would cover. Two buttons raise made-up events: the patient moving toward the edge of the bed, and something left in a clear area. Each lights its place and puts a notice in front of staff and on the clinician workstation, which stays until a person acknowledges it. Reset takes the events away. The readings it lists are the ones the room already has.
features.benefit: Staff would be told where to look, without more alarms or more screens.
features.awake: Nothing about it is shown to the patient.
features.sedated: The bed's edge is the event staff would care about most.
features.limits: A concept for monitoring and decision support, not a validated clinical device. Nothing watches or listens: no camera, no microphone and no sensor reading; every event is a button. It changes no alarm or device, and it isn't AI.

features.name: Room safety scan
features.purpose: Check a room digitally before it's built: the items a visitor places, against the space that care needs.
features.how: Under Place items, run the room safety scan. It runs the same check the Future ICU fittings passed on the room as the visitor has arranged it: each placed item against the keep-clear areas round the bed, the space in front of each door, the wardrobe's front and the walking route to the bed, and against everything solid. Green: no modelled conflict found. Amber: a clearance to look at. Red: an overlap. Choose a result to read why, with the item lit and a nearby clear spot marked on the floor. The visitor moves the item, and the scan runs again.
features.benefit: Conflicts show up while the room is still a drawing.
features.awake: Nothing about it is shown to the patient.
features.sedated: Nothing about it is shown to the patient.
features.limits: The areas are this model's own, set as data and illustrative: green means no modelled conflict found, never that a room is safe, and it isn't a compliance check against hospital rules.

features.name: Ceiling pendant
features.purpose: Ceiling services: the monitor, the pumps and the outlets hang from the ceiling at the bed head, so the floor round the bed stays clearer and the essentials are within reach.
features.how: The pendant in the room model carries the patient monitor, the infusion pumps, shelves and power, data and gas outlets. With the cable channels on, its services come down from flush channels in the ceiling, power and data in one and medical gas in another. Equipment labels name it, and the cable overlay shows what runs through it.
features.benefit: The kit staff reach for is at the bed head, off the floor, and the floor is easier to clean.
features.awake: It sits behind the patient's head, out of their way.
features.sedated: Staff reach the outlets and pumps from either side of the bed.
features.limits: A visual model of a pendant, not a specified product. Its position, load, services and the ceiling's structure would need engineering, infection-control and clinical review.

features.name: Cables and channels
features.purpose: Less clutter, better access and safer movement: the cables and lines round the bed shown by kind, loose and then organised.
features.how: Under Equipment and cables, Traditional shows today's arrangement: power, data and gas cables loose on the floor from the wall to the kit. Organised shows them routed: power and data in one flush channel, medical gas in its own, down the ceiling pendant, and the ventilator on a docking spot fed from the pendant, so nothing crosses the floor. Each kind has a label in the room as well as a colour. The patient's own lines are the bed's (clips and tags) and APIS's (Tubing & movement): linked, not repeated.
features.benefit: Staff can see where each cable runs before a move creates a hazard.
features.awake: Nothing about it is shown to the patient.
features.sedated: Nothing about it is shown to the patient.
features.limits: Illustrative routes, not an engineering or clinical design. Nothing retracts, clamps or disconnects a line, and nothing moves by itself. Medical gas and electrical services would need their own engineering and regulatory review.
